title: Stablecoins could put Australia's $24 billion digital finance opportunity within reach
full_text:
This content has been provided by a third party.
Australia's financial system is approaching a moment where the mechanics of moving money could become as important as the money itself.
A March 2026 report from the Digital Finance Cooperative Research Centre https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/03/02/australia-could-unlock-ausd24-billion-in-digital-finance-gains-is-on-track-for-just-ausd1-billionestimated that digital finance innovation could generate around A $24 billion in annual economic gains, equivalent to roughly 1% of GDP. Yet the same research found Australia could capture only about A$1.1 billion a year by 2030 on its current trajectory.
The gap has put payment infrastructure firmly inside a much larger conversation about productivity.
The DFCRC attributes the potential gains to tokenization across financial markets, payments and assets, with foreign exchange alone accounting for an estimated AUD$7.2 billion in annual opportunity. https://dfcrc.com.au/2025/06/16/au-19-billion-per-year-economic-impact-could-be-unlocked-through-digital-finance-innovation-new-research/ The research points to regulatory uncertainty and limited pathways from experimentation to scaled deployment as obstacles to capturing the full value.
Policy activity is now catching up with technology. The House Economics Committee's A Level Playing Field https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/House_of_Representatives/About_the_House_News/Media_Releases/A_Level_Paying_Field_Economics_Committee_releases_report_on_the_Australian_payments_sectorreport recommends that Treasury establish a framework enabling stablecoins as an alternative payment rail within Australia's payments system "as a matter of urgency." The recommendation places stablecoins inside the architecture of payments policy, giving the technology relevance far beyond the crypto market.
The Reserve Bank of Australia has also moved the discussion into its next phase. Following Project Acacia, a joint RBA and DFCRC initiative involving experiments with tokenised assets and different forms of digital money, the central bank launched a September 2026 consultation examining how its settlement infrastructure could support tokenised finance.
Project Acacia identified potential gains from faster settlement, reduced counterparty risk and greater capital efficiency.
Drew Bradford, CEO of Macropod, views stablecoins through this infrastructure lens. His argument centres on how money moves through the economy, with stablecoins functioning as payment tokens that could give banks another mechanism for transferring value.
"Stablecoins are payment mechanisms. They're not a financial service in itself. They're not a financial security, they're not a deposit, they're a payment," Bradford explains. "Stablecoins are a payment token. They move faster, they're cheaper, and they're programmable, which normal money can't be any of those three."
That distinction matters most in cross-border payments, where traditional settlement processes can introduce delays and costs. Bradford argues that stablecoins could allow international transfers to happen around the clock, including weekends, while reducing the friction associated with conventional banking networks.
"You can send money offshore. You can transfer from Australian dollars to sterling, Australian dollars to US dollars instantly," he says.
"At the moment, to transact that via normal banking rails it takes 24 hours, 48 hours, 72 hours, depending, But with Stablecoins you can send money on Saturday afternoon instantly."
The potential economic impact also extends into the machinery sitting behind transactions. Bradford argues that businesses should focus closely on savings generated through blockchain settlement, particularly across post-trade processes.
"A lot of people, when they see something new, they say, 'How much money am I going to make? They don't look at how much money I am going to save," he explains. "The amount of money you will save is massive. It's not a 5 per cent reduction in cost; it's an 85 per cent reduction in cost."
Banks therefore have a practical role in the transition. Bradford argues that institutions could incorporate stablecoins into existing offerings, giving customers access to faster payment infrastructure while retaining the broader banking relationship.
"Banks should use them because it's better than sending money via their correspondent network, which they do today," he says. "Because of this, stablecoins are something that banks should care about and not view as a threat, but view as an enhancement to their current product base."
Australia's policy challenge now concerns execution. Project Acacia https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/tokenised-money/project-acacia/has already moved the conversation from theoretical possibilities into tested use cases, while the RBA's latest consultation is examining the infrastructure required to support tokenised markets.
Bradford sees stablecoins as an entry point into a wider transformation of financial infrastructure.
"The productivity gains available to Australia from adopting stablecoins and adopting tokenization are worth north of $24 billion a year," he argues.
"The starting point is stablecoins instead of using traditional old money. This is a new way of doing things: faster, cheaper, better."
The AUD$24 billion figure belongs to the DFCRC's broader digital finance research, not to stablecoins alone. For payments, the significance lies in the infrastructure that could help Australia capture those gains.
Stablecoins form one component of that emerging architecture, putting the focus firmly on a more consequential question: how quickly can Australia turn financial experimentation into usable infrastructure?
